w: Poland's biggest amusement park sits inside Silesian Park's 26 hectares, drawing a quarter-million visitors a year by the late 2000s. A Slovak resort operator bought it in 2015, renamed it Legendia, and rethemed its rides and attractions around folklore and legend.
s: Amusement park rethemed around local legend
_facts: located within Silesian Park, area of 26 ha
2008: 253,000 visitors
acquired in 2015 by Slovakian company Tatry Mountain Resorts, renamed Legendia, themed to "Legends"

w: At 620 hectares - twice the size of New York's Central Park - this is one of Europe's largest urban parks, built to restore land devastated by industry in a heavily urbanized region. A 1990s land swap during Katowice's Millennium district construction left it entirely within Chorzow's borders.
s: Reclaimed industrial land, twice the size of Central Park
_facts: 620 hectares, twice as large as Central Park in New York
restored an industrially devastated piece of land in a highly urbanized area
exchange of land during construction of the Millennium district in Katowice in the 1990s left it entirely within Chorzow, though it belongs to no single district

w: Katowice's museum dedicated to the history and culture of Silesia. The public record on its holdings stays spare, but as the region's namesake museum, it's an obvious starting point for anyone tracing Upper Silesia's story.
s: Katowice's museum of Silesian history and culture
_facts: a museum in the city of Katowice, Poland

n: Christ the King Cathedral in Katowice
w: Poland's largest cathedral took 28 years to build, from 1927 to 1955, funded by the autonomous Silesian Parliament between the wars. Pope John Paul II visited in 1983 and sat on a throne still displayed in its dedicated chapel today. Faced in stone over brick, the cathedral is also renowned for its acoustics.
s: Poland's largest cathedral, visited by a pope
_facts: constructed 1927-1955, funded by the autonomous Silesian Parliament
the largest archcathedral and cathedral in Poland, 120,000 cubic metres
visited by Pope John Paul II in 1983, whose throne is on display in a dedicated chapel
faced in stone but built of brick, known for high-quality acoustics

w: Three concrete wings rake skyward near the Spodek arena, each one standing for a Silesian Uprising - 1919, 1920, 1921 - fought to bring Upper Silesia into the newly independent Polish state. Unveiled in 1967, its slopes are etched with the names of the battles fought there, funded by the people of Warsaw.
s: A wing for each Silesian Uprising, 1919-1921
_facts: monument to the three Silesian Uprisings of 1919, 1920 and 1921, aimed at making Upper Silesia part of Poland
unveiled 1 September 1967, designed by Gustaw Zemla and Wojciech Zablocki
wings symbolize the three uprisings, names of battle sites etched on the slopes
funded by the people of Warsaw

w: Katowice's central square dates to the late 19th century and has been rebuilt more than once, including demolitions under communist rule for modern service blocks. Streetcar tracks cross it in several directions, and every noon a bugle call - a tradition invented only in 2002 - sounds from a tenement rooftop.
s: A 2002-invented noon bugle call sounds daily
_facts: dates to the late 19th century, rebuilt several times
during the communist era historic buildings were demolished for modern service facilities
streetcar tracks cross the square in several directions
a noon bugle call, a tradition created only in 2002, is played from a tenement rooftop

w: Poland's largest residential building when it opened in 1972, designed as an architectural counterpart to the Spodek arena and inspired by Le Corbusier's Unite d'habitation. Its 762 flats have windowless kitchens and wall-integrated heating - the radiators, so the story goes, simply never arrived on schedule.
s: Brutalist giant with windowless kitchens by design
_facts: one of the largest residential buildings in Poland, the largest when built in 1972
intended as an architectonic counterpart to Spodek, inspired by Le Corbusier's Unite d'habitation
762 residential flats, small windowless-kitchen flats meant for singles/couples
heating integrated into the walls without visible radiators, chosen because planned radiator elements were not delivered on time

w: Completed in 1900 in an eclectic mix of Gothic Revival and Renaissance Revival styles, Katowice's Great Synagogue served its Jewish congregation for less than four decades before Nazis burned it down in early September 1939, in the invasion of Poland's opening days. Nothing of Max Grunfeld's design survives.
s: Synagogue burned by Nazis in the 1939 invasion
_facts: designed by Max Grunfeld in an eclectic Gothic Revival and Renaissance Revival style, completed 1900
destroyed by Nazis by arson in early September 1939, during the invasion of Poland

w: One of the oldest buildings in Katowice, this wooden log church didn't start out here at all - it was originally built in the village of Syrynia in 1510 and physically relocated to Kosciuszko Park in 1938. Its free-standing belltower, historic lych-gate and wooden churchyard fence all predate the move by centuries.
s: A 1510 wooden church, relocated whole in 1938
_facts: one of the oldest buildings in Katowice
moved to Kosciuszko Park in 1938 from the village of Syrynia, where it was built in 1510
free-standing belltower completed before 1679, historic lych-gate and wooden fence around the churchyard

w: A 35-metre lattice tower built in 1937 to train paratroopers - and, within two years, pressed into a very different role. When Germany invaded in 1939, its 73rd Infantry Division used the tower as an observation post. It's the only parachute tower left standing in Poland.
_facts: 35-metre tall lattice parachute tower built in 1937 for training parachute jumps
used in the first days of WWII by Germany's 73rd Infantry Division as an observation tower
the only existing parachute tower in Poland

w: Four generating units went up here between 1985 and 2000, coal-fired and still carrying a heating capacity of 200 MWt. What catches the eye is the 200-metre flue gas stack bristling with antennas - an industrial-age landmark you can spot from across the city.
_facts: coal-fired power station consisting of four units built 1985-2000
heating capacity of 200 MWt
flue gas stack is 200 metres tall, equipped with several antennas

w: Housed within the Tyskie brewery complex and opened in 2004, this museum is an official anchor point on the European Route of Industrial Heritage and a listed national monument. In a 2009 public vote, the brewery was named one of the Seven Architectural Wonders of the Silesian Voivodeship.
s: Industrial-heritage museum inside a working brewery
_facts: established 2004, Anchor point on the European Route of Industrial Heritage
object of cultural heritage in Silesia and a Polish national monument
voted one of the Seven Architectural Wonders of the Silesian Voivodeship in 2009

w: Founded in 1823 by Scottish engineer John Baildon at Friedrich Wilhelm von Reden's invitation, this steelworks anchored Katowice's Zaleze and Dab districts for generations. Its 2001 closure triggered one of Poland's largest labor protests since the 1980s: 2,500 steelworkers marched for their jobs.
s: 1823 steelworks whose closure sparked mass protest
_facts: founded 1823 by Scottish engineer John Baildon, invited by Friedrich Wilhelm von Reden
located in the Katowice districts of Zaleze and Dab
major local employer until liquidation in 2001
2001: 2,500 steelworkers staged one of the largest demonstrations in Poland since the 1980s
